<p><strong>Summary</strong>:</p>
<p data-pm-slice="1 1 []">Researchers demonstrated an analog phase-change memory architecture that stores multiple AI vectors in superposition, increasing effective storage density with a tunable accuracy tradeoff. Tests on prototype PCM hardware showed inference accuracy close to full-precision software.</p>

		<title>The imec Report: Scaling Optical Interconnects For The AI Era</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/the-imec-report-scaling-optical-interconnects-for-the-ai-era/</link>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Unprecedented demand for bandwidth calls for bringing optics closer to silicon through a fundamental rethinking of the optical interconnect roadmap.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-imec-report-scaling-optical-interconnects-for-the-ai-era/">The imec Report: Scaling Optical Interconnects For The AI Era</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The explosive growth of cloud computing and AI – from generative, and reasoning, to (ultimately) agentic systems – is creating unprecedented demand for bandwidth, as the amount of data that must be moved both within and between data centers continues to surge. In turn, this exposes growing limitations in the underlying interconnects that not only span the data center fabric and rack level but also extend deep inside servers – down to where they link XPUs, memory, and other system components at the package and die level.</p>
<p><strong>Copper-based (electrical) interconnects</strong> have long been the industry’s workhorse thanks to their low cost, simplicity, and reliability. Yet today, they are increasingly hitting fundamental limits: while highly energy-efficient electrical links can be realized, they are typically confined to very short reaches (on the order of millimeters). At longer distances and higher lane rates, power consumption rises sharply, thermal constraints intensify, and signal integrity degrades. In other words, electrical I/O is rapidly becoming a key barrier to scaling next-generation AI and machine learning systems.</p>
<p><strong>Optical interconnects</strong> have emerged as a critical path forward. By transmitting data using light rather than electrical signals, they are far less sensitive to distance, enabling much better energy efficiency while mitigating many of the crosstalk and thermal challenges inherent to copper links. However, even optical technologies are now being pushed to new extremes – as the need emerges for (multi) terabit-per-second interfaces, ultra-high energy efficiency, and extremely low (sub-microsecond) latency.</p>
<p>Meeting these requirements will take more than incremental innovation. It calls for a fundamental rethinking of the optical interconnect roadmap; one that progressively brings optics closer to the silicon – from the front panel, into the package, and ultimately firmly integrated into the wafer stack.</p>
<h2>Pluggable optics (PO): The longstanding – and still very much alive – workhorse</h2>
<p>For more than two decades, <strong>pluggable optical transceivers</strong> have been the backbone of high-speed telecom and datacom networks – powering everything from enterprise workloads and video streaming to today’s hyperscale cloud infrastructure. Inserted into standardized ports on switches, routers, and servers, pluggables convert electrical signals from the host into optical signals for transmission over fiber – and back again on the receive side.</p>
<p>They deliver:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Modularity and flexibility</strong> – optics can be upgraded independently of the (electrical) host.</li>
<li><strong>Serviceability</strong> – pluggables are hot-swappable, meaning they can be replaced without system downtime.</li>
<li><strong>Multi-vendor interoperability</strong> – achieved via IEEE 802.3 standards, and through widely-adopted multi-source agreement (MSA) form factors such as QSFP, QSFP-DD, and OSFP.</li>
<li><strong>Thermal stability</strong> – the optical engine sits in a front-panel cage, physically separated from the power‑dense ASIC; this helps protect lasers, modulators, and photodetectors from excessive heat (improving reliability).</li>
</ul>
<p>Across successive generations, pluggable optical transceivers have scaled from 100/200G to 400G and 800G by pushing baud rates (the number of symbols transmitted per second on a single optical lane), adopting higher-order modulation (such as PAM-4), and increasing the number of parallel lanes.</p>
<p>And despite their maturity, pluggable optics continue to evolve. First-generation <strong>1.6T pluggable transceivers</strong>, for instance – relying on 200Gbps per-lane data rates, combined in an eight-lane parallel architecture – are approaching sampling and early deployment, targeting direct-reach (DR) intra-data center links as well as forward-reach (FR) connections over single-mode fiber.</p>
<p>The key enabler is <strong>silicon photonics (SiPho)</strong>, which underpins this scaling through a combination of (silicon-based) optical and electronic building blocks, including Mach–Zehnder modulators that play a central role in enabling cost-effective 200Gbps per-lane operation while keeping power consumption in check.</p>
<p>Looking further ahead, toward the end of the decade, the industry is eyeing the <strong>3.2T pluggable optics </strong>milestone. Yet, achieving these performance levels will require continued advances in high-speed electronics, packaging, and thermal management – as well as a substantial expansion of the silicon photonics (SiPho) toolbox. On the transmit side, for instance, optical modulators will need to support bandwidths beyond 100GHz while maintaining low insertion loss and high modulation efficiency – requirements that are becoming increasingly difficult to meet with conventional silicon devices alone.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283328" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=906%2C445&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="906" height="445" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?w=906&amp;ssl=1 906w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C147&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C377&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C295&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 906px) 100vw, 906px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Pluggable optics have delivered an order-of-magnitude leap in performance in the past few years – both in bandwidth density and power efficiency. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>Addressing these limitations is driving interest in the <strong>heterogeneous integration of higher-performance electro-optic materials</strong> such as lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃). Techniques such as <strong>micro-transfer printing</strong> offer a promising path to integrate these materials onto silicon photonics platforms. Early results are encouraging, but further research is ongoing to scale these approaches to high-volume manufacturing – so that future 3.2T modules can be built with the same practicality, reliability, and cost discipline that made pluggable optics the industry’s workhorse in the first place.</p>
<p>In parallel, alternative scaling approaches are also being explored. Concepts such as <strong>extreme pluggable optics (XPO)</strong> target capacities up to 12.8T by further increasing bandwidth density, albeit at the expense of significantly higher system complexity and the need for liquid cooling, which – at least for now – impacts both cost and practical deployment.</p>
<h3>A double world-first: Integrating LiNbO₃ and LiTaO₃ on SiPho via micro-transfer printing</h3>
<p>As optical interconnects (need to) push beyond today’s 200Gbps-per-lane standard, GeSi-based devices increasingly struggle to deliver the required combination of bandwidth and energy efficiency. While GeSi modulators have demonstrated scaling to 400Gbps per lane in the C-band, such performance has not yet been achieved in the O-band. To unlock the next performance leap in pluggable optical interconnects, researchers are therefore investigating the heterogeneous integration of advanced electro-optic materials – such as lithium niobate (LiNbO₃) and lithium tantalate (LiTaO₃) – onto silicon photonics, paving the way for a new class of high-speed modulators and photodetectors.</p>
<p>A promising enabler is <strong>micro-transfer printing</strong>, which enables the precise placement of thin-film materials onto SiPho wafers without the material waste, post-bonding complexity, and cost typically associated with conventional wafer bonding. Two world-first results highlight its potential:</p>
<p>First, researchers from imec and Ghent University showcased an O-band 320Gbps unamplified optical link over 2km of single-mode fiber. This was achieved using a high-bandwidth 100GHz germanium photodiode in combination with transfer-printed thin-film lithium niobate Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs), integrated onto a SiPho platform and co-packaged with custom-designed traveling-wave drivers and TIAs. This work marked the first seamless integration of LiNbO₃ modulators onto a silicon photonics platform using micro-transfer printing.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283329" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=1544%2C1030&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1544" height="1030" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?w=1544&amp;ssl=1 1544w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C200&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C683&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C512&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=1536%2C1025&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C400&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: The first seamless integration of LiNbO₃ modulators onto a silicon photonics platform using micro-transfer printing. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>The team also achieved the first-ever heterogeneous integration of a LiTaO₃ modulator on a silicon photonic integrated circuit. Using the same micro-transfer printing technique previously applied to lithium niobate, the researchers achieved full compatibility with the entire wafer stack, enabling co-integration with other photonic building blocks such as heaters, filters, and germanium photodetectors without compromising their performance.</p>
<p>While these modulators are still relatively large, they offer a viable path for further scaling pluggable transceivers, where footprint constraints are less stringent. At the same time, alternative device concepts are being explored to meet the tighter size and integration requirements of future <strong>co-packaged optics</strong>. These include compact, ultra-high-speed GeSi-based modulators operating in the C-band, as well as emerging approaches based on the integration of III-V materials into silicon photonics platforms.</p>
<p>Further work is required to scale these heterogeneous integration approaches to high-volume manufacturing. Nevertheless, the results highlight a promising route toward integrating &gt;100GHz electro-optic devices on SiPho – a capability widely seen as essential for future 3.2T pluggable modules and next-generation optical interconnects supporting AI-driven infrastructure.</p>
<h2>Fast-and-narrow co-packaged optics (CPO): A key pillar of the optical interconnect roadmap</h2>
<p>Pluggable optics, however, are not the answer to every challenge. The rapid rise of (generative) AI workloads is pushing optical (inter)connectivity ever deeper into compute servers and accelerator clusters – all the way down to the chip-to-chip level.</p>
<p>At this scale, a new set of constraints emerges. Pluggable optical transceivers rely on very high baud rates, in combination with sophisticated digital signal processing (DSP) to compensate for signal degradation. While this works well at the rack or data center level, the power consumption and latency associated with heavy DSP become increasingly problematic for short-reach, <strong>chip-to-chip optical interconnects </strong>in AI and machine learning systems. Instead, they require intrinsically clean optical channels with extremely low bit-error rates, allowing each lane to operate without excessive equalization or DSP overhead.</p>
<p>This shift is precisely what drives the adoption of <strong>fast-and-narrow co-packaged optics (CPO)</strong>. In a CPO system, the optical components are placed in close physical proximity to the (switching) silicon or compute die, shrinking the electrical path from several centimeters (as in pluggables) to just a few millimeters – or even less. By moving the electro-optic conversion point directly adjacent to the ASIC (within the same package), CPO greatly improves signal integrity, minimizes electrical losses, and reduces latency – without relying on power-hungry DSP. This makes CPO a compelling architecture for scaling next-generation AI and high-performance compute systems.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283330" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=1202%2C598&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1202" height="598" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?w=1202&amp;ssl=1 1202w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=300%2C149&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=1024%2C509&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=768%2C382&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig3.webp?resize=600%2C299&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Co-packaged optics shorten the electrical path between the optical engine and the host IC, enabling higher bandwidth density and eliminating the need for digital signal processing, thereby improving power efficiency. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>But as early CPO deployments begin to emerge, integration complexity remains one of the defining challenges of the technology. Unlike pluggable optics – where the optical module is (largely) self-contained – CPO requires <strong>tight co-design and co-optimization</strong>, including photonic integrated circuits (PICs), electronic ICs (EICs), switch ASICs, fiber‑coupling strategies, thermal management, and advanced packaging. Addressing this multidisciplinary challenge is a central objective of imec’s Optical Interconnect Program.</p>
<p>In the CPO domain (also referred to as OIO2.5D), imec’s key research targets include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Scaling optical engine capacity from 1.6T and 3.2T, toward 6.4T and ultimately 12.8T.</li>
<li>Enabling fast-and-narrow 400Gbps lane rates, and achieving bandwidth densities approaching 1Tbps per millimeter.</li>
<li>Facilitating energy efficiencies up to 5pJ/bit, trending toward 3pJ/bit in future technology generations.</li>
<li>Integrating the full optical stack – modulators, photo detectors, couplers, fiber attach, and thermal solutions – within a manufacturable package.</li>
</ul>
<p>Reaching these targets depends heavily on advanced semiconductor packaging technologies that support dense integration of photonic and electronic components – think of 2.5D interposer architectures, through-silicon vias (TSVs), fan-out wafer-level packaging (FO-WLP), and (increasingly) 3D integration enabled by hybrid bonding – as well as the use of advanced (III-V) materials.</p>
<p>And then there’s the light source. While the long-term goal is to integrate lasers directly on the photonic chip, early CPO systems will still rely on <strong>externally mounted laser sources</strong>. This approach simplifies thermal management and mitigates long-standing reliability concerns of operating lasers near hot ASICs. The trade-offs: higher output power to compensate for optical losses, greater packaging complexity, and the need for additional fibers and connectors to route light into the package.</p>
<h3>Realizing the first net-400Gbps per-lane transmission with a silicon-based EAM</h3>
<p>In October 2025, imec announced a major advance for next‑generation optical interconnects: a beyond-110GHz C-band GeSi electro-absorption modulator (EAM) delivering a net data rate of 400Gbps per lane.</p>
<p>Leveraging the Franz-Keldysh effect, the device combines compact size, high speed, and low power consumption. And thanks to its GeSi foundation, it integrates seamlessly on 300mm CMOS-compatible SiPho platforms, offering a clear route to high-volume manufacturability.</p>
<p>This breakthrough reflects more than a decade of coordinated progress at both the device and system levels. On the device side, imec optimized footprint, doping schemes, and epitaxial growth processes. At the system level, a robust PAM-4 IM/DD transmission setup validated sustained net-400Gbps per-lane operation, demonstrating the practical readiness of GeSi EAM technology for future high-lane-rate optical engines.</p>
<h2>3D integrated optics (OIO3D): The next frontier</h2>
<p>As AI and machine learning systems scale to thousands of tightly interconnected accelerators, each linked to high-bandwidth memory stacks and peer processors over distances of only a few millimeters, the demands placed on optical interconnects become even more extreme. Over the next decade, they are expected to support bandwidth densities approaching (and surpassing) 10Tbps/mm, energy efficiencies well below 1pJ/bit, and ultra-low latencies (&lt;100ns). These targets extend beyond what even advanced CPO architectures can achieve.</p>
<p>To meet these requirements, optics must move beyond the package and into the wafer stack itself. This is the foundation of <strong>3D integrated optics</strong>. By collapsing the electrical path to micrometer-scale distances, OIO3D enables ultra-short, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient optical links that make dense chip-to-chip optical fabrics feasible.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283331" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=1202%2C606&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1202" height="606" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?w=1202&amp;ssl=1 1202w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=300%2C151&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=1024%2C516&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=768%2C387&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_scaling-optical-interconnect-AI-fig4.webp?resize=600%2C302&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 4: By collapsing the electrical path to micrometer-scale distances, OIO3D enables ultra-short, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient optical links that make dense chip-to-chip optical fabrics feasible. Source: imec.</strong></p>
<p>Realizing 3D integrated optics requires overcoming several major technology challenges. These include scalable laser integration, the development of high-efficiency, high-bandwidth electro-optic components (e.g., based on GeSi, lithium niobate, lithium tantalate, indium phosphide, or barium titanate), and robust thermal management in densely stacked environments. Equally crucial are ultra-precise bonding and alignment techniques at wafer scale.</p>
<h3>OIO2.5D vs OIO3D</h3>
<p>An evolutionary step beyond CPO, <strong>OIO2.5D</strong> combines high‑density photonic integration with manageable packaging complexity by placing photonic and electronic dies side‑by‑side on a shared silicon interposer. Photonic layers are integrated using die‑to‑wafer Cu‑based hybrid bonding, a technique that enables ultrashort, low‑parasitic electrical paths.</p>
<p>This architecture initially targets optical engines in the 8-32Tbps range. It leverages 32-64 Gbps per‑lane rates, optimized for low‑power, DSP‑free operation to minimize latency and heat. Wavelength‑division multiplexing (8-32 wavelengths per fiber) further boosts aggregate bandwidth without increasing fiber count. The technology roadmap aims for bandwidth densities of 2Tbps per millimeter and energy efficiencies near 2 pJ/bit.</p>
<p><strong>OIO3D</strong> represents the most advanced and ambitious vision for optical interconnects. Here, photonic layers are stacked directly above or below the compute silicon, creating a true chip‑scale optical fabric that collapses electrical paths to micrometer‑scale distances.</p>
<p>This approach relies on both die‑to‑wafer and wafer‑to‑wafer hybrid bonding, enabling extremely fine‑pitch vertical interconnects. With this level of vertical integration, OIO3D aims to extend bandwidth capabilities to tens of terabits per second (and beyond), while targeting energy efficiencies around 2 pJ/bit – with a longer‑term trajectory toward sub‑pJ/bit operation.</p>
<p>A key research vector is on‑wafer laser integration, using heterogeneous III‑V approaches such as quantum‑dot GaAs‑on‑Si. This is actively being explored within the EU Chips Act pilot lines for future large‑scale photonic systems.</p>
<h3>Integration of barium titanate on a 300mm SiPho platform</h3>
<p>In January 2026, Veeco Instruments Inc. and imec announced a 300mm high-volume-manufacturing-compatible process for integrating barium titanate (BaTiO<sub>3</sub>, BTO) on silicon photonics.</p>
<p>With exceptional electro-optic properties, BTO enables high-speed, low-power modulators for applications ranging from optical transceivers to quantum photonics, LiDAR, and AR/VR. Historically, however, bringing BTO to silicon at scale has been difficult due to cost, uniformity, and manufacturability constraints.</p>
<p>Leveraging a collaboration with imec, Veeco recently delivered its first molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) cluster system tailored for 300mm wafers. The platform supports the growth of single-crystalline BTO thin films on silicon – using solid and hybrid MBE – improving repeatability, material quality, and cost of ownership compared with conventional MBE solutions.</p>
<h2>A look at timelines</h2>
<p>Looking across the evolution of optical interconnects, it is clear the different approaches are progressing along different timelines.</p>
<p><strong>Pluggable optics</strong>, already deployed at global scale, are entering a phase dominated by incremental technical optimizations rather than fundamental breakthroughs. Their roadmap continues – toward 1.6T and 3.2T modules – and pluggables will remain competitive for many use cases while new architectures ramp up.</p>
<p><strong>Co-packaged optics</strong> are also approaching a stage of (relative) maturity. Key building blocks are transitioning into pilot-line support, supply-chain preparation, and wafer-level services – even as the industry continues to pursue higher bandwidth, faster lane rates, and better energy efficiency. The start of broad, large-scale CPO deployments is expected from 2027/2028 onward.</p>
<p><strong>3D integrated optics</strong> remain in an earlier R&amp;D stage. Current efforts focus on pathfinding and building the device/integration toolbox. First proof-of-concept demonstrators are anticipated within three to five years, with wider commercialization expected on a five- to ten-year horizon.</p>
<h3>Bringing next-generation optical interconnects to market</h3>
<p>Through its <a href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/expertise/cmos-advanced/connect/optical-interconnects">optical interconnects research program</a>, imec develops the key building blocks for future optical transceivers, anticipating market needs years before commercial deployment.</p>
<p>Imec’s strength lies in being a true one-stop R&amp;D environment, bringing together expertise in silicon photonics, advanced CMOS, 3D integration, materials research, and system-level modeling. This breadth allows researchers to explore novel concepts far more rapidly than is possible in high-volume manufacturing settings, enabling short development cycles, and the freedom to pursue unconventional (integration) approaches. The program is further strengthened by imec’s <a href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/expertise/cmos-advanced-and-beyond/xtco">cross-technology optimization (XTCO)</a> strategy, which drives scaling across technology domains.</p>
<p>A critical accelerator is the close collaboration between imec’s optical interconnect research teams and <a href="https://www.imeciclink.com/en">IC-Link</a>, imec’s semiconductor manufacturing pillar. While imec’s early‑stage research focuses on pathfinding and prototyping, IC‑Link helps bring technologies toward higher technology‑readiness levels by refining process flows, improving manufacturability, establishing test strategies, and engaging the broader supply chain. Through IC-Link, industrial partners can also access and evaluate these technologies via imec&#8217;s 200mm and 300mm iSiPP silicon photonics platforms, providing a pathway from early-stage innovation to industrial deployment.</p>
<p>Beyond IC-Link, imec maintains close engagement with industrial partners through a variety of collaboration models. These span guided projects (in which imec and its partners jointly explore emerging technologies), to targeted bilateral programs (driven by partner-specific requirements), all the way to long-term core partner engagements. In parallel, imec collaborates closely with equipment suppliers, enabling early validation of advanced tools and process capabilities – well before they enter commercial use.</p>
<p>Together, these interactions ensure that imec’s optical interconnect research stays firmly grounded in real‑world system requirements, while accelerating the translation of advanced technologies into market-ready solutions.</p>
<p><em>Peter Ossieur received the M.Sc. degree in electrical engineering from Ghent University, Belgium in 2000, and the PhD degree in electrical engineering from the same university in 2005. From 2005 till 2009 he was a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University, after which he joined Tyndall National Institute, where he became senior staff researcher. His research interests included electronic integrated circuit design and optical transmission systems. In 2017, he joined imec-IDlab, an imec embedded group at Ghent University. Today, he is director for XTCO Fabric and Optical Interconnect at imec, and holds a parttime appointment as professor at Ghent University. Peter Ossieur is a member of the ISSCC wireline subcommittee.</em></p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>imec</strong> published “Beyond HBM-on-GPU: Thermal Design Envelope for 3D Volumetric DRAM-on-GPU Integration.”</p>
<p><strong>Summary</strong>:<br />
Researchers evaluated a 3D memory architecture that rotates DRAM dies vertically above a GPU and places cooling cavities between them as an alternative to conventional 2.5D HBM and direct-stacked HBM-on-GPU. Package-level thermal simulations examined stack height, memory capacity and organization, cooling-cavity materials, stack orientation, mold insertion, and the addition of a distributed memory-controller/network-on-chip tier.</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24343">technical paper here</a>. September 2026</p>
<p>Chen, Yukai, Melina Lofrano, Khakim Akhunov, Jonas Svedas, Arjun Singh, Nathan Laubeuf, Diksha Moolchandani et al. &#8220;Beyond HBM-on-GPU: Thermal Design Envelope for 3D Volumetric DRAM-on-GPU Integration.&#8221; arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.24343 (2026).</p>

		<title>Large-Format Masks Move From Aspiration To Industry Roadmap</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/large-format-masks-move-from-aspiration-to-industry-roadmap/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/large-format-masks-move-from-aspiration-to-industry-roadmap/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Jan Willis]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 07:02:08 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Meet The eBeamers]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[curvilinear]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[D2S]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Dai Nippon Printing]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[DNP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[eBeam Initiative]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[EUV]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[high-NA EUV]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[HJL Lithography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[large-format masks]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Micron Technology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[photomasks]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24283279</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Expert panel sees a compelling productivity case, but the entire photomask ecosystem must be ready together.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/large-format-masks-move-from-aspiration-to-industry-roadmap/">Large-Format Masks Move From Aspiration To Industry Roadmap</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The eBeam Initiative conducted its 15th annual Luminaries survey in July and reported the results on September 9, 2026, at its annual reception during the SPIE Photomask Technology + EUV Lithography Conference. 85 luminaries representing more than 45 companies participated.</p>
<p>At the close of the annual eBeam Initiative reception, an expert panel discussed a number of survey results, including large-format masks, equipment investment, High-NA EUV, and curvilinear masks. Moderator Aki Fujimura, CEO of D2S and co-founder of the eBeam Initiative, was joined by Harry Levinson of HJL Lithography, Naoya Hayashi, DNP Honorary Fellow, and Glen Scheid of Micron Technology (pictured in Figure 1). In this blog, I&#8217;ll report key insights shared by the panel.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283280" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?resize=2048%2C1073&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2048" height="1073" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?w=2048&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?resize=300%2C157&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?resize=1024%2C537&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?resize=768%2C402&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?resize=1536%2C805&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig1-panel.webp?resize=600%2C314&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: eBeam Initiative Luminaries Survey Results Discussed by Expert Panel (left to right, Aki Fujimura, Naoya Hayashi, Harry Levinson, Glen Scheid) </strong></p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): 66% of luminaries predicted that the industry will adopt a large-format mask – approximately 6 x 12 inches – within the next decade. The survey was completed before TSMC and ASML announced an industry initiative targeting a 12-inch mask pilot line by 2031. Why is this transition happening now?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: The wafer fab argument is productivity. High-NA EUV systems are extremely expensive and occupy valuable cleanroom space. A large-format mask can expose a larger field without the process-control complexity of A/B stitching, with the potential for roughly 40% better productivity. That is a significant advantage when each additional system also adds facilities and power requirements.</p>
<p><strong>Scheid</strong>: The alignment forming around the 12-inch format is exciting. Mask-size transitions are extremely rare, and this one has a clear productivity benefit that the industry needs.</p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): Harry, you were involved in the industry&#8217;s earlier attempt to standardize a nine-inch mask. Why is this different?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: The nine-inch proposal came from extrapolating historical growth in DRAM die size. The intended customers did not plan to build dies that large, so the format solved no real problem and was rejected. This time, the demand is coming directly from chipmakers. Intel initiated the discussion, and now TSMC, ASML, and other companies are supporting it. The application and the value are clear.</p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): What must happen across the supply chain to meet the 2031 pilot-line target?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Hayashi-san</strong>: The whole ecosystem must be ready at the same time. Some critical parts of the mask-making chain have only one supplier. We need to watch the ecosystem carefully and support the areas that could prevent the complete process from being available when it is required.</p>
<p><strong>Scheid</strong>: This is a collective schedule, not a set of individual schedules. The combined probability of success falls as the number of required elements grows. One late supplier – especially in a single-source area – can delay the transition. Redundancy can reduce risk, but this is a small industry, and the investment may be too large to support two suppliers in every category.</p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: There are financial and technical risks. Some tools may require a larger stage and different handling, while processes such as uniform etching deserve closer attention. Funding risks should be addressed early, especially for smaller suppliers. Companies planning fabs around this timing will worry about whether every element will arrive on schedule.</p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): What new manufacturing challenges come with a rectangular mask that has twice the area?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Hayashi-san</strong>: Processes based on spinning become more difficult. Resist coating, development, cleaning, and drying all must remain uniform across a larger rectangular surface. The longer edges and corners can create water-drop issues at the corners, so these processes will need deep evaluation.</p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: It took roughly 15 years to make EUV multilayer films suitable for high-volume manufacturing. Much of that learning will transfer, but scaling the multilayer blank will not be as simple as installing a few larger tools.</p>
<p><strong>Scheid</strong>: More mask area means more opportunity for particles, while contamination and cleaning already are leading EUV mask-lifetime concerns according to another survey result. A large-format pellicle could help in the fab, but the mask shop still must clean a larger surface with uniform chemistry and without adding defects.</p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): Has High-NA EUV moved from a question of if to a question of when?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: Yes. Only a year ago, people still asked whether High-NA was real. Now it is in production at Intel along with publicly announced roadmaps from multiple companies, which is a sea change. Samsung announced they will be in production with High-NA by 2028 and TSMC said they intend to use it in high-volume manufacturing for advanced nodes starting in 2030. Beyond High-NA, demand is less certain. Device and interconnect engineers first must show that smaller features provide the required performance.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283281" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig2-survey.jpg?resize=1300%2C731&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1300" height="731" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig2-survey.jpg?w=1300&amp;ssl=1 1300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig2-survey.jpg?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig2-survey.jpg?resize=1024%2C576&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig2-survey.jpg?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/eBeam_Large-Format-Masks-Roadmap-fig2-survey.jpg?resize=600%2C337&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: 2026 eBeam Initiative survey result predicting equipment purchase in the next three years.</strong></p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): 68% of luminaries expect mask-etching-system purchases to increase over the next three years (Figure 2). What is driving that result?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Scheid</strong>: Purchases of multi-beam writers and inspection tools are predicted to increase over the next three years and reflect both capacity growth and capability needs. Etching is different. New High-NA mask materials may not be compatible with existing systems or with .33 NA materials running side by side. The survey prediction that etching tool purchases will increase in the next three years is less about adding etch capacity and more about adding new capability.</p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: At the same time, uniformity requirements are tightening. Improving uniformity while introducing new materials makes etching a very active development area.</p>
<p><strong>eBeam Initiative (Fujimura): What about curvilinear wafer targets?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Scheid</strong>: Curvilinear masks are already here, enabled by multi-beam writers and supported by formats such as MULTIGON. Full layers with curvilinear wafer targets automatically generated are harder to see within a three-year window.</p>
<p><strong>Levinson</strong>: The benefits demonstrated for curvilinear wafer features are compelling, although backside interconnect and other changes make the timing uncertain. On the mask side, curvilinear is here now and will continue to grow stronger.</p>
<p><strong>Hayashi-san</strong>: Writing curvilinear masks with a multi-beam writer is straightforward. Qualification remains a challenge, but the level of attention at this conference shows that the industry is working on it.</p>
<p>The panel&#8217;s conclusion was optimistic, but not complacent. The productivity case for large-format masks is strong, High-NA is now in production as well as in roadmaps from two more companies, and mask shops are investing in new equipment and curvilinear masks. The difficult part will be coordinating the complete ecosystem. This industry&#8217;s history of solving shared technical challenges may be its most important advantage on the road to 2031.</p>
<h3>Reference links:</h3>

		<title>Testing Silicon Photonics At Scale</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/testing-silicon-photonics-at-scale/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/testing-silicon-photonics-at-scale/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Clemens Leichtle]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 07:01:58 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Connect With SEMI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Advantest]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[photonics]]></category>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24283273</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>New test requirements include fiber alignment, coupling efficiency, polarization management, and optical instrumentation.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/testing-silicon-photonics-at-scale/">Testing Silicon Photonics At Scale</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) are driving unprecedented demand for data movement. As bandwidth requirements climb and conventional electrical interconnects encounter limitations in power consumption, latency and reach, silicon photonics, near-packaged optics (NPO), and co-packaged optics (CPO) are becoming increasingly important technologies for next-generation data centers.</p>
<p>Much of the industry’s attention has focused on photonic device innovation. But demonstrating a high-performance photonic integrated circuit (PIC) is only part of the challenge. Turning these devices into products that can be manufactured reliably and economically at high volume requires a test infrastructure that can keep pace.</p>
<p>This represents a significant shift. Semiconductor manufacturing has benefited from decades of refinement in automated electrical test. Silicon photonics adds an optical dimension that brings new requirements for fiber alignment, coupling efficiency, polarization management, and optical instrumentation—while still requiring conventional electrical characterization.</p>
<p>As silicon photonics moves from development environments toward high-volume production, test becomes more than a quality gate. It is an integral part of the manufacturing strategy.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24283274 size-full" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig1.webp?resize=1428%2C747&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1428" height="747" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig1.webp?w=1428&amp;ssl=1 1428w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C157&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C536&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C402&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C314&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: An HVM-ready test solution requires a full complement of supporting hardware and software.</strong></p>
<h2>Bringing precision optical alignment to production</h2>
<p>One of the most fundamental challenges is establishing a reliable optical connection to the device under test. Unlike electrical probing, where physical contact provides a relatively straightforward interface, optical testing depends on precisely coupling light into and out of very small structures.</p>
<p>That coupling must be repeatable from device to device and wafer to wafer. Even small variations in fiber position or angle can affect insertion loss and measured optical performance, potentially making it difficult to distinguish actual device variation from variation introduced by the test setup.</p>
<p>For this reason, high-volume testing requires automated alignment capabilities that can quickly locate the optical interface and optimize coupling. This can involve visual or image-based positioning to bring a fiber array unit close to the grating couplers, followed by area scans and gradient-search techniques to identify the optimal position via feedback loops – a technique typically referred to as “active alignment.” The process may also require optimization across six degrees of freedom—X, Y, and Z positioning plus three rotational axes—to maximize coupling efficiency and minimize channel-to-channel variation.</p>
<p>The problem becomes more complex as optical interfaces add channels. Alignment must not simply maximize one channel&#8217;s performance; it must produce consistent coupling across multiple channels. Rotational alignment, for example, can influence how evenly an optical beam overlaps multiple grating couplers. Other angular adjustments can affect both insertion loss and center wavelength.</p>
<p>Polarization presents another variable. Because photonic structures can respond differently depending on the polarization state of incoming light, polarization must be characterized and controlled as part of a repeatable production methodology. Together, these requirements make alignment an active measurement and optimization process rather than a simple mechanical positioning step. The manufacturing challenge is to automate these functions without allowing alignment time to become a throughput bottleneck.</p>
<h2>Combining electrical and optical test without sacrificing throughput</h2>
<p>Alignment is only one part of the equation. A PIC may incorporate photodetectors, modulators, and other components requiring combinations of optical and electrical measurements. Typical characterization can include insertion loss, channel-to-channel uniformity, optical attenuation, photodetector responsivity, and wavelength-dependent behavior.</p>
<p>Performing these measurements sequentially can add substantial test time. A more scalable approach is to integrate electrical and optical capabilities so that operations can occur concurrently wherever possible. For example, electrical alignment can occur before optical alignment, while continuity and other electrical tests may run during automated optical probe alignment rather than waiting for that process to finish. This type of parallelism becomes increasingly important as device complexity and test coverage grow.</p>
<p>The same principle applies to optical instrumentation. Rather than treating each instrument as an isolated resource, high-volume environments benefit from integrated control of lasers, power meters, and other optical equipment, enabling parallel operation of multiple instruments or channels. Automated calibration and compensation are also important for maintaining measurement consistency as the test cell becomes more complex. Advantest’s development work in this area supports multiple optical instruments and parallel power-meter operation within a common test environment.</p>
<p>The broader objective is familiar from semiconductor test: maximize useful test coverage while minimizing test cost. What changes with silicon photonics is the number of physical and measurement domains that must be coordinated to achieve it.</p>
<h2>Collaboration will be essential to ecosystem scaling</h2>
<p>No single supplier controls all of the elements required for high-volume PIC test. The complete solution can span automated test equipment, wafer probing, optical positioning, fiber interfaces, optical instrumentation, device design, and manufacturing processes.</p>
<p>That makes ecosystem collaboration particularly important. Test equipment providers need to work with probe and positioning specialists, photonic device developers, foundries, and manufacturers so the interfaces among these technologies function as an integrated production system rather than individual laboratory instruments.</p>
<p>As an example, Advantest has collaborated closely with FormFactor to develop a wafer-level photonics test environment that combines electrical test instrumentation with wafer handling, optical instruments, and automated fiber alignment capabilities. The significance lies less in individual components than in the integration required to create a repeatable manufacturing workflow.</p>
<p>As silicon photonics, NPO and CPO move toward broader adoption, these collaborative efforts will become increasingly important. The industry must develop practical test methodologies that accommodate evolving device architectures while delivering the repeatability, throughput, and economics expected of semiconductor manufacturing.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283275" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=2560%2C869&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2560" height="869" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?w=2560&amp;ssl=1 2560w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=300%2C102&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=1024%2C348&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=768%2C261&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=1536%2C522&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=2048%2C696&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SEMI_Testing-Silicon-Photonics-at-Scale-fig2-scaled.webp?resize=600%2C204&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Numerous photonics developments on the horizon will require broad industry effort to bring to fruition.</strong></p>
<p>The transition from promising photonic technology to high-volume commercial products will depend on more than advances in the devices themselves. Test must evolve alongside them. By treating optical alignment, electrical and optical measurement, automation, and ecosystem interoperability as parts of a single manufacturing challenge, the industry can build the infrastructure needed to bring silicon photonics fully into the era of high-volume production.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/testing-silicon-photonics-at-scale/">Testing Silicon Photonics At Scale</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Bringing Down Test Costs For Co-Packaged Optics</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/bringing-down-test-costs-for-co-packaged-optics/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/bringing-down-test-costs-for-co-packaged-optics/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Laura Peters]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 07:01:57 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Round Tables]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Test, Measurement and Analytics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Advantest]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ASE]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CPO]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[failure analysis]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ISE Labs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Keysight Technologies]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[near packaged optics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[NPO]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[standards]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Teradyne]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[test costs]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24283051</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Pinpointing failures, ensuring known-good optical engines, and controlling test costs become increasingly critical as photonics moves into advanced packages.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/bringing-down-test-costs-for-co-packaged-optics/">Bringing Down Test Costs For Co-Packaged Optics</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>For FA, engineers need to identify boundaries and be able to decouple individual components to identify the root cause of problems.</li>
<li>Underperforming lasers are a substantial issue, making the “golden reference” a hot topic in test.</li>
<li>Training in electro-optics is critical to understanding tradeoffs in design and test.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p><strong>Experts At The Table</strong>: Testing cost for optical components is high, approaching the manufacturing cost. Loopback capability is an important part of failure diagnosis. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/teradyne-corporation/">Teradyne</a>; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/advantest-corporation/">Advantest America</a>; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/ase/">ASE Group</a>; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight Technologies</a>. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click <a href="https://semiengineering.com/cpo-testing-faces-a-moving-target-problem/">here</a>. Part two is <a href="https://semiengineering.com/scaling-cpo-testing-beyond-a-single-die/">here</a>.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282423" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?resize=1768%2C548&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1768" height="548" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?w=1768&amp;ssl=1 1768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?resize=300%2C93&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?resize=1024%2C317&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?resize=768%2C238&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?resize=1536%2C476&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-05-at-4.54.22-PM.png?resize=600%2C186&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal</strong></p>
<p><strong>SE:</strong> <strong>How do you determine where failure originates in electro-optical systems?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Yamaguchi</strong>: We always look at the reference plane. For the testing, these are the physical, electrical, and optical boundaries at each of the measurement planes — for example, determining where this boundary sits. Is it at the die pad, package balls, the connectors, or the fiber interface? We also need to think about de-embedding everywhere between the boundaries — for instance, probe, socket, trace, connectors, patch cord — whatever we are introducing, and making sure the same boundaries are used at testing insertions 1, 2, and 3. We need to align those boundary conditions, as well. So then we emulate the missing half. For example, to test the optical engine alone, you replace the neighbors with a known characterized substitute. If we have a golden reference laser source, that can be used.</p>
<p><strong>Griffin</strong>: We are seeing customers add monitor photodiodes into their light paths, so that if they see an unexpected result from the transmit or receive path, they can trace it back. Some customers doing loopback testing want tap capability so they can route to characterization instrumentation or simply monitor power. That&#8217;s useful if they aren&#8217;t planning to do a full characterization test and just want to do loopback or mission-mode testing. The downside is that if it fails and you don&#8217;t meet your bit error rate or you have a functional issue with the program, you may not know why. So being able to tap into that loopback capability could be important.</p>
<p><strong>Leventhal</strong>: I wanted to follow up about having a golden reference for a laser source. Really, the job at the end of the day is not to test the laser source. We&#8217;re looking for how to test the part. That laser source is basically the functional equivalent of the device power supply on the electrical side, and we don&#8217;t call that a golden reference. We call it a device power supply, and it&#8217;s a given that thing is supposed to work as it should, just like everything else in the test system. Customers want to default to getting the laser source out of the equation and to use the same one that they&#8217;re using in mission mode, but that laser source is not an ATE instrument, so things are going to need to evolve. As Dave talked about, FA is following your nose, and you need to be able to discern the scent of things that should be in the equation of causing trouble and things that should be just off the table because it’s a given they’re known-good.</p>
<p><strong>SE:</strong> <strong>In what ways is co-packaged optics (CPO) failure diagnosis harder than near-packaged optics (NPO) FA?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Griffin</strong>: When people say NPO and CPO, there isn&#8217;t always a standard definition of those terms. The two share similar challenges, in that module test requires alignment of multiple optical connectors, and we still need to deliver power to the device. Some customers will say, ‘With NPO, I can detach the optical engines.’ That might be a key distinction. So you could argue that the test coverage before that attachment becomes less valuable, because if I detect a failure caused by a bad optical engine, I can just remove it. But we&#8217;ve also heard from customers that reworking and reattaching further downstream is a real pain point, which means they still want known-good optical engines, regardless of detachability.</p>
<p><strong>Leventhal</strong>: With CPO, you have a lot more stuff integrated onto the package, and you need to have ways of decoupling them. And so many of the themes that we&#8217;ve talked about over the course of this discussion come into play here. DFT would help, as Dave discussed — understanding what information you need to get out of the testing on the individual pieces so you can correlate it to what&#8217;s going to fail in the package.</p>
<p><strong>Yamaguchi</strong>: A retimed NPO has its own DSP, so the optical engine can be compliance-tested on its own, like a pluggable, and a failure is easy to locate. A linear-drive NPO removes the DSP, and the host ASIC SerDes drives the optics directly through linear drivers and TIAs (transimpedance amplifiers). The electrical and optical sides then form one signal path, so a failed link can&#8217;t easily be traced to either side. The test complexity is the same as for CPO.</p>
<p><strong>Armstrong</strong>: Another concern is high power dissipation. For CPO, your electrical signals can&#8217;t drive very far, and hopefully with an NPO they can. And because you have higher reach in the electrical, you have to manage that. The thermal of all these optical parts is a big deal.</p>
<p><strong>SE:</strong> <strong>How does the economics of tests change when you have an inexpensive photonics device integrated with a very expensive ASIC or GPU?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Leventhal</strong>: You can’t have an inexpensive optical engine taking down a $40,000 or $50,000 GPU or ASIC, so it&#8217;s an interesting change in terms of your test budget. We tend to look at test costs as a certain percentage of the manufacturing cost of that chip, but this blows that completely out of the water. Now you essentially have like an infinite test budget for these chips that are going to surround your big ASIC. Of course, you always look for ways to reduce test cost, but you do have the ability to over-test at the beginning to make sure that you&#8217;re not throwing away the really expensive chip. And then, over time, we will get the yield learning information as we scale.</p>
<p><strong>Yamaguchi</strong>: The device value is increasing, the scrap cost is increasing, the test complexity is increasing, the package complexity is increasing. So, given this situation, additional wafers or optimal engine-level testing become more justifiable, and that&#8217;s how the economics are shifting toward pre-assembly screening rather than packaging test, which we have traditionally served in the industry.</p>
<p><strong>Griffin</strong>: I completely agree. I would add that the end customers for these AI accelerator and network switch devices are highly motivated to deploy as many of these as possible into data centers so they can generate more tokens. These are some of the most complex semiconductor devices ever made. If you look at the cost of an optical engine in isolation, you get a different answer than if you look at the extremely complex package that it&#8217;s going to be integrated into, and the core functionality it provides. It reduces power and enables disaggregated compute architectures, which makes that device extremely critical. So we&#8217;re going to see continued focus on testing these systems efficiently.</p>
<p><strong>Leventhal</strong>: For the industry, it&#8217;s no longer a challenge to prove that CPO works. Meta presented strong reliability data earlier this year showing it&#8217;s actually quite reliable. It works. Now the question is, &#8216;How do you take what we have today to high-volume manufacturing?&#8217; That&#8217;s an ecosystem problem. It&#8217;s not just a problem in a single piece of the puzzle. So we&#8217;ll deal with that in the shorter term by relying on additional testing, screen-in, burn-in, more insertions, more engineering controls, while the ecosystem gets dialed in and matures. NPO plays a really important role in this. It&#8217;s a lower hurdle to jump over to get up and running. Learnings that come out of that will bootstrap efforts to bring CPO to HVM. But it won&#8217;t be a slam dunk. And you asked what we haven&#8217;t talked about at this point. The answer is standards. The industry is moving so fast that standards bodies can&#8217;t keep up. Where standards come into play is not to invent the technology, but to be able to manufacture at scale, where we have multiple sources for parts.</p>
<p><strong>Yamaguchi</strong>: The industry is looking into standards and MSAs to enable the technology and collaborate with ecosystem partners. Standards don’t change the measurement science itself, but they align the platforms, and that is where the industry can help most. Some of the test criteria also include questions like how much optical power needs to be transmitted and what kind of bias you need to apply. That helps us prepare the manufacturing requirements and the deliverables.</p>
<p><strong>Griffin</strong>: With almost every customer we talk to, there are two different groups within that company — the photonics group, which has been testing devices but typically not at the scale of semiconductor high-volume manufacturing, and the semiconductor high-volume test group. The test group is really concerned about uptime, software support, service support, ensuring they can deploy many test cells in high volume, and there are a lot of decisions you would make about a test cell for flexibility, modularity, and serviceability that may force a trade-off on optical performance. So from an ecosystem perspective, these groups have to talk to each other within the company to make educated decisions regarding acceptable trade-offs. No one knows their device better than the customer, the designers, and the manufacturing teams, so they need to understand that if I choose a certain connector type for more flexibility or higher channel count, but it results in slightly lower optical power at the DUT, that may impact the design. These conversations require multiple groups at the same company with vastly different backgrounds talking to each other, and I think we&#8217;re just now starting to see that happen because the production ramp is starting. Those conversations will do more to move the industry forward than anything else.</p>
<p><strong>Armstrong</strong>: According to the surveys we&#8217;ve done in the IPSR, the cost to test an optical component is approaching the cost of manufacturing, and as the complexity rises, it may exceed the cost of manufacturing. That means the industry will have to realize that they&#8217;re going to have to pay for quality and known-good die, and as Ira alluded to, there should be money on the table because the reality is the cost of testing the GPU on a percentage basis is peanuts compared to the cost of testing the optical components. So the economies have to shift a little bit, and there could be different companies involved. Also, it takes a community. Each of us needs to work with partners to grow a structure that makes sense for all of us to help the industry move forward in a unified, consistent fashion that is scalable and high-volume production-capable.</p>
<hr />
<p><strong>Read parts one and two of the discussion:</strong><br />
<a href="https://semiengineering.com/cpo-testing-faces-a-moving-target-problem/">CPO Testing Faces A Moving Target Problem</a><br />
Test vendors are adapting to changing connector architectures and extreme alignment tolerances as co-packaged optics heads toward mainstream.</p>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/scaling-cpo-testing-beyond-a-single-die/">Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die</a><br />
Fiber alignment, connector durability, and simultaneous optical and electrical testing pose challenges for high-volume manufacturing.</p>

]]></content:encoded>

<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/self-heating-and-parasitics-challenge-multi-tier-cfet-scaling-tu-munich-iit-kanpur/">Self-Heating And Parasitics Challenge Multi-Tier CFET Scaling (TU Munich, IIT Kanpur)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at the <strong>Technical University of Munich</strong> and <strong>Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur</strong> published “Self-Heating and Parasitic Effects in Multi-Tier CFET Design.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt</strong>:<br />
&#8220;We study the impact of self-heating effects (SHEs) and middle of line (MOL) and back-end of line (BEOL) induced parasitics on multi-tier CFET design, where multiple nanosheet devices are vertically stacked. We analyze and compare the four-tier complementary FET (CFET) design with the conventional two-tier CFET, using TCAD models calibrated to experimental measurements. In addition, TCAD simulations are used to model and analyze SHE-induced heat distribution and temperature profiles and to extract the detailed parasitic RC network from 3-D models of CMOS inverters designed with full MOL and BEOL interconnects.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11569014">technical paper here</a>. June 2026</p>
<p>Shahin, Sufia, Mahdi Benkhelifa, Yogesh Singh Chauhan, and Hussam Amrouch. &#8220;Self-Heating and Parasitic Effects in Multi-Tier CFET Design.&#8221; IEEE Journal on Exploratory Solid-State Computational Devices and Circuits 12 (2026): 153–158. https://doi.org/10.1109/JXCDC.2026.3704373. <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">License</a>.</p>

In a phone interview with EE Times, Arm CMO</p>]]>
